It's not too different in some respects to the Spanish conquest of south America. Current south Americans are largely indigenous in overall autosomal* ancestry(at least outside of the southern cone) yet in terms of paternal lineages alone(Y chromosome) as well as language and culture, the impact of the colonizers was much greater. The expansion of aryans was kinda similar. They moved in new places, conquered the locals and took their women as wives, imposing to a large degree their language, culture and paternal lines via a clannish, patriarchal system. The more the areas they conquered were populated, the smaller the overall replacement was i.e bronze age Greek speaking Mycenaeans in Greece were give or take ~15% steppe. In poorly populated north Europe on the other hand, people from Corded ware culture could be way more than 50% steppe. And indeed modern north Euros are ~50% steppe, give or take ~5/10%. Similarly in Indus Valley and Iran, these areas were heavily populated already, so overall these incomers from the north didn't cause an overall huge shift in ancestry.

*autosomal simply means ancestry over all of the 22 pairs of non-sexual chromosomes. Sexual chromosomes only take a very small part of the overall DNA, the Y chromosome is the smallest of all, but it has the important property that it isn't subject to recombination like the others i.e it's essentially inherited in total from the father alone, so while it isn't useful to track things like phenotype, it is useful to track things like migrations. Autosomal on the other hand recombines with ancestry from both parents, so the women have an important role in it.

There's few variables you should tweak:

  • hirisplex_csv_path: this is just the path of the standard hirisplex-S file you can download from the site, it's needed mostly to assemble the final input csv

  • snps_bed_path: this contains the actual bed-like file describing the SNPs to query and is also used by bcftools to annotate the pileup file; since the annotate function seems quite hard to work with, I'm pasting you the file itself in the format it seems to like: https://pastebin.com/kZpUmYTZ

this was obtained in any case using the biomaRt library and the hg19 dbSNP list

  • sratools_path, samtools_path, bcftools_path: these are just the paths to the respective executables; sratools_path is only needed if you plan to let it automatically download from SRA; if you are using pre downloaded BAMs you won't need it

  • hg19_path: just the path to the hg19.fa needed for calling/alignment

  • pos_window: this is basically the width/2 of the region to query either from SRA or from the BAM; e.g say you want to check for rs683 at 12709305 in chr9, if pos_window is 200, then the script is going to query the region chr9:12709105-12709505 and so on for every other snp; I included this variable just to be sure, I don't know exactly how much a bigger window can influence the calling, I think 200 is more than enough

  • wait_time: this is only needed for SRA automatic download; it is just the waiting time in seconds between two sra-dump calls; unfortunately, this software doesn't seem to have the option to download from multiple regions at once, so I have to call it for each single region and since this involves download from the net I opted for a waiting time between the various downloads

this is going to create a bunch of SRA_snp#.sam and SRA_snp#.bam files in the directory from which you call the script, which the script is going to merge into one full.bam file before doing the calls

the function you are interested in is pheno_query(sample_id, sample_name, nochr_flag, fullbam_flag); this function should, if all goes correct, produce a hirisplex_in.csv file to input in the site;

it has basically two modes, which are selected by setting the flag fullbam_flag to either TRUE or FALSE

if set to TRUE, then it's going to interpret the sample_id variable as the path to the BAM; if FALSE then it's going to interpret sample_id as the SRA run number

sample_name is just the final name to give to the sample;

nochr_flag is important: some BAMs have chromosomes in the format chr#, others just #, without the "chr"; hg19.fa, at least the one I have, is in chr# coordinates, so if needed the software will do a reheader call to set things straight before doing the rest

if your BAM(or SRA file) is NOT in the format chr#, then set nochr_flag to TRUE and the script is going to fix it; otherwise, if it's already in chr# format, set it to false

you can check if what you have is in either format with a 'samtools view file.bam' call(if you have the full BAM already) or online in the SRA run page

for example, say you want to check the phenotype of Villabruna: on SRA, its run number is ERR1341842, so if I want to make the script download from there automatically, I'm going to call pheno_query("ERR1341842", "Villabruna", TRUE, FALSE); I set nochr_flag to TRUE since they have it in the # chromosome format;

but say instead you have the full BAM downloaded already, maybe from ENA; then you run it like so: pheno_query("path to full BAM", "Villabruna", TRUE, TRUE)

the pheno_table and pheno_table_files functions are just to create a png of the single individual in the first case and a list of individuals in the second(like I did above); the first takes as input the Result.csv file from the hirisplex site; the second one takes as input a one per line list of paths to Result.csv files to assemble into one
